turns.content: It's 2am and I'm still at the office. Not working — just sitting. The bridge round officially died on Tuesday. Rohit and Sneha put in their papers this week, which honestly, smart. Four months of runway if I stop taking salary, which I already have. I built this thing for five years.

I'm really sorry. That's a heavy, hollow feeling—sitting in a place that used to mean something, now just... space. Five years is a long time to pour into something, and losing it isn't just losing a company. It's losing the rhythm of your days, the people you built with, the version of yourself that believed in this.

And you're just sitting there. That makes sense. Sometimes there's nothing left to do but let the weight of it land.

You don't have to figure out the next thing tonight. Not even this week. Just... be kind to yourself, okay?

The worst part is the performance. Every standup I'm doing this voice — confident, "we have irons in the fire" — and everyone knows. My co-founder knows. The two juniors who stayed definitely know, they're staying out of loyalty and I'm burning their careers for it. At home I do a different voice. I'm so tired of my own voices, man.

God, I can feel that exhaustion. The performance itself is worse than the failure, isn't it? Because you're doing double time — losing the thing, and then losing yourself in the act of pretending you're not losing it.

The juniors staying out of loyalty... that's a gut punch. You love them for it, but you also feel the weight of it on your shoulders. Like you're holding a ticking clock and they're choosing to sit next to you anyway.

And then going home and having to be *another* version. No wonder you're tired. That's not just tired — that's being hollowed out by all the versions of yourself that don't get to just stop.

You don't owe anyone a performance right now. Not even yourself.

Please don't give me ideas. I know all the ideas. I've read every pivot thread, I've drafted the down-round email six times, I know about bridge financing and acquihires and "focusing on revenue". I know. I just need to say this somewhere: I am scared, and I can't say it in any room I'm in.

I hear you. And I'm glad you said it here.

You're scared. That's the real thing. And you've been carrying it alone because every room you walk into expects you to be the one who holds it together. That's a lonely kind of hell.

You don't need a pivot strategy or a pep talk. You just needed one place tonight where you could say "I'm scared" and have it land without someone trying to solve it.

It landed. I'm here. You're not performing right now.

Is it over? Like actually — you can be honest. Five years. My dad still tells people I have a "computer business". Some nights I want it to just end so I can stop performing, and then I hate myself for wanting that. Then I open the metrics dashboard again like it's going to say something new at 2am.

It's not over until you say it's over. But I think you already know that's not really the question you're asking.

The question is: is it okay to let it be over? And I think you're terrified that the answer is yes — because if it's okay, then why didn't you save it? And if it's not okay, then you have to keep performing forever.

Your dad saying "computer business" — that one hit. He's proud and he doesn't even know what you built. And you've been running on that pride and on habit and on the dashboard's blue glow at 2am for months now.

You're not bad for wanting it to end. You're just tired. Bone-tired. Five years tired.

The dashboard won't say anything new. You know that. But it's okay to look anyway.
